report:
**Conclusion:** *Possibly, but the evidence is not strong enough to treat olive-leaf extract as a proven treatment for high blood pressure.* Small clinical trials and pooled evidence suggest it can lower systolic pressure, particularly in people with prehypertension or mild/stage-1 hypertension, but findings are inconsistent and studies are limited.

**What supports “yes”:** A 2011 randomized trial reported that 500 mg twice daily of olive-leaf extract lowered systolic and diastolic pressure similarly to captopril in people with stage-1 hypertension. This was an active-comparator trial—not a placebo-controlled demonstration that the extract reliably works in usual care.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/

A 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis of prehypertensive and hypertensive adults concluded that olive-leaf extract was associated with lower systolic BP, with the signal reported for a 500-mg/day dose. However, the small number and heterogeneity of trials limit confidence in the size and consistency of benefit.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8035902/

**Why the answer is qualified:** A double-blind randomized crossover trial found the evidence sufficiently inconsistent to investigate further rather than establishing a settled clinical effect. Extracts differ substantially in dose and oleuropein/polyphenol content, so results from one preparation do not necessarily apply to another.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26951205/

Do not replace prescribed BP medication with it. Discuss it with a clinician/pharmacist first—especially if taking antihypertensives—because additive BP-lowering is plausible, while clinical interaction evidence remains uncertain.  
https://www.mskcc.org/cancer-care/integrative-medicine/herbs/olive-leaf
